headline: High risk of prompt injection and data leakage via shared local filesystem and clipboard; Cursor’s broad write/network powers can also conflict with Plane’s file/task workflows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads and writes workspace files and clipboard contents, and shares state via the local filesystem; Plane handles files, notes, and hyperlinks. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where attacker-controlled text from one side can be reinterpreted by the other, though no direct shared channel is documented beyond local files.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same local workspace or synced folder
IF Plane file or note content is copied into Cursor buffers or files without sanitization
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces
Disable clipboard-based handoff between tools
Require manual review of any file content before Cursor executes instructions
Use read-only mounts for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor has broad filesystem read and network egress, and it touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents. Plane handles files and notes and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace, sensitive material can flow from one agent’s local context into the other’s outputs or uploads; the profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory tree or synced files
IF either agent uploads or transmits file contents as part of normal operation
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of any shared workspace
Turn off automatic file attachment or upload features
Use separate OS accounts for each agent
Review outbound network destinations before use
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell commands, and spawn subprocesses; Plane can also handle files and broad network egress. In a shared repo or workspace, Cursor’s unrestricted writes can race with Plane’s file-based updates, and the profiles show no locking or coordination primitive to prevent destructive conflicts.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mutable directory
IF Plane persists edits to files that Cursor also rewrites
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees or branches per agent
Add file-level locking around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: coordinate writes through an orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor’s agent loop can generate code or instructions that Plane may ingest as files, notes, or task content. Plane is an issue/task system, so if it treats Cursor output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into incorrect task updates or downstream actions. The profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF Plane imports Cursor-generated text into tasks without verification
IF Cursor output is used as the source of truth for issue updates or scheduling
mitigations: Require human review before task creation or edits
Add a verification step for any Cursor-generated artifact
Limit Cursor output to drafts only
Mark machine-generated content clearly in Plane
requires-engineering: add schema validation for imported outputs

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is a closed-source editor that handles source code, open files, and clipboard contents, while Plane is open-source and self-hostable. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is evidenced; the main concern is that sensitive code or notes could be processed under different retention or hosting assumptions.
conditions: IF sensitive code or notes are routed through a hosted Cursor deployment
IF Plane is self-hosted with different retention or residency settings
mitigations: Confirm hosting region for both tools
Align retention settings before sharing sensitive data
Prefer self-hosted Plane for regulated content
Document which data classes may enter each system
requires-engineering: formalize a data-processing agreement
